clue.text: Something one just has to have

definitions.text: Something one just has to have

parts.words: Something one just has to have
parts.note: surface reading: an essential item nobody can do without
setter's reading: the abstract state of having or possessing a thing

explanation.surface: A shopper insists some gadget is an absolute must-buy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has to have' sounds like necessity, but read literally it is simply 'having', the condition of possessing something.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names the legal state of possessing property, the thing a person has.

clue.text: Refuse to abandon Irish county finally?

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it behind, so a letter of the county is dropped
'finally' says which letter goes: the closing one of the county name

parts.note: Offaly is a county in the Irish midlands

explanation.surface: Someone declines to leave an Irish county at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb but is the noun, rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun once meant waste or rubbish; the word comes from 'off-fall', the parts cut away.

clue.text: Teachers ignored inadequate service, served vegetarian meal

parts.note: the National Union of Teachers
to cut someone is to snub them
in tennis a let is a serve that clips the net and must be replayed

explanation.surface: Staff at a school canteen put up with poor service and dished up a meat-free dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUT was the main British teachers' trade union.
explanation.definitionFit: A patty of chopped nuts shaped like a meat chop is a traditional meat-free main course.

clue.text: To do this to her clues, editor intervenes

definitions.text: To do this to her clues, editor intervenes

indicators.note: to intervene is to come between, so the editor goes inside the reordered letters
the answer itself means rearrange, so doing it to the words reorders their letters

parts.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A puzzle editor steps in to rejig a setter's clues.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: an editor stepping in to rearrange a setter's clues is exactly what the answer describes.
explanation.definitionFit: To rearrange the order or timing of something is to set it out on a new plan.

clue.text: Get sharper about sinful bishop setting example for the cloth

indicators.note: 'about' means the word for sharpen wraps around the next pieces

parts.note: to hone is to sharpen
erring means straying into sin
chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A wayward bishop sharpens up and sets an example to the clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: H(ERRING B)ONE. 'The cloth' suggests the clergy, but here it is fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: A zigzag weave resembling fish bones is a common pattern woven into tweed and other fabrics.

clue.text: Touring Spain, start off garbling Spanish and grad-ually make progress?

indicators.note: touring means travelling around, so the mixed letters go around the country code
garbling jumbles words, so the remaining letters are mixed up
the opening letter is taken off the nationality

parts.note: taken as written
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

explanation.surface: A traveller in Spain mangles the language at first but slowly improves.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'grad-ually' hints at a graduate easing into a job step by step.
explanation.definitionFit: To introduce something in stages means bringing it into use a step at a time.

clue.text: Some prickly characters created scenes in Channel Islands

indicators.note: 'in' places the word for the scenes inside the islands' abbreviation

parts.note: standard abbreviation for the Channel Islands
to act up is to make a scene

explanation.surface: Awkward people causing scenes in Jersey or Guernsey.
explanation.walkthrough: C(ACT)I. 'Prickly characters' suggests touchy people, but the setter means spiny desert plants.
explanation.definitionFit: These spiny succulent plants are literally covered in sharp spines, a playful use of the word for touchy people.

clue.text: Old radio component, not quite the best

indicators.note: 'not quite' means the phrase stops one letter short of its full length

parts.note: 'the cat's whiskers' is slang for the very best

explanation.surface: A vintage wireless part that falls just short of top quality.
explanation.walkthrough: The bee's knees and the cat's whiskers both mean the very best.
explanation.definitionFit: Early crystal radio sets used a fine wire touching a crystal, nicknamed after a feline's facial hair.

clue.text: Religious belief expressed by socialist in company

indicators.note: 'in' places the political word inside the business abbreviation

parts.note: standard abbreviation for company
red is the traditional colour of the left

explanation.surface: A leftist in a business voices a creed.
explanation.walkthrough: C(RED)O.
explanation.definitionFit: A creed is a statement of faith, from the Latin 'I believe' that opens Christian creeds.

clue.text: Does he appear silly, playing cricket?

definitions.text: Does he appear silly, playing cricket?

parts.note: surface reading: someone looks foolish while playing
setter's reading: silly point and silly mid-on are fielding positions close to the bat

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a cricketer looks daft on the field.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, 'silly' fielding positions are those very close to the batsman, near the middle of the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A fielder stationed close to the batsman is a fielder in the near ring rather than out on the boundary.

clue.text: Clot, however, begins to identify one of these goddesses

parts.note: surface reading: someone stupid nevertheless starts to recognise something
setter's reading: the letters 'Clot' start the name of one of the goddesses, Clotho

explanation.surface: A dimwit finally begins to recognise one of a group of goddesses.
explanation.walkthrough: Clotho, the spinner of the thread of life, is one of the three Fates of Greek myth; her name begins with 'Clot'.
explanation.definitionFit: Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos are the three Greek goddesses who spin, measure and cut the thread of life.

clue.text: Complain and criticise, starting Sunday dinner?

indicators.note: 'starting' tells us the word for criticise must come first, ahead of the word for complain

parts.note: to roast someone is to criticise them harshly
to beef is slang for to grumble

explanation.surface: A grumpy guest moans and finds fault before tucking into the weekend meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Without 'starting' the parts would read in clue order; it moves criticise to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint of meat cooked in the oven is the classic British Sunday lunch, given here by example.

clue.text: Given extra volume about precipitation? It amplifies what's been said

indicators.note: 'about' means the word for extra volume goes around the weather word

parts.note: made louder
hail is a form of precipitation

explanation.surface: Something turned up loud during a hailstorm boosts the speech.
explanation.walkthrough: LOUD(HAIL)ER.
explanation.definitionFit: A megaphone device makes a speaker's voice carry further, amplifying their spoken words.

clue.text: See 4
Plays may be in production by this August

definitions.text: Plays may be in production by this August

parts.words: Plays may be in production by this August
parts.note: surface reading: theatre shows will be staged by late summer
setter's reading: August is a first name, that of a Swedish dramatist

explanation.surface: A theatre promises its new shows will be running by next month.
explanation.walkthrough: August Strindberg (1849-1912) was the Swedish dramatist of Miss Julie; 'August' looks like the month.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swedish dramatist's plays, such as Miss Julie, are still regularly staged.

clue.text: Hound rapid progress, as controller of papers

parts.note: a bulldog is a breed of dog
to move at a clip is to go quickly

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor races ahead, hounding staff like a press baron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hound' looks like a verb meaning harass, but it is the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The spring-loaded metal fastener grips a stack of loose sheets together, keeping them under control.

clue.text: Support hospital facilities getting into a worse state

parts.note: to back is to support
a hospital is divided into wards

explanation.surface: Funding for hospital units lets them decline further.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads as 'going backwards', so the answer works as an adverb of decline.
explanation.definitionFit: Going in reverse means regressing, slipping back to a poorer condition.

clue.text: Fellow holding a fit of pique back, where details can be recorded?

indicators.note: 'back' tells us the whole assembled string reads from right to left
'holding' means the fellow's word wraps around the following phrase

parts.note: a don is a university fellow
taken as written
a pet is a sulk or fit of bad temper

explanation.surface: A sulky academic jots down the particulars of his grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: DON holding A PET makes DAPETON, which reversed gives NOTEPAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A pad of paper sheets is a place to write down notes and particulars.

clue.text: Cope with freak storm? An aspect of self-control

indicators.note: a storm throws things into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Handling a freak storm calmly shows self-control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aspect' is meant as a look on the face.
explanation.definitionFit: An expressionless look that hides one's feelings, as card players keep, shows composure and restraint.

clue.text: Tom may leave at this point, as Queen makes an entrance

definitions.text: Tom may leave at this point, as Queen makes an entrance

parts.words: Tom may leave at this point, as Queen makes an entrance
parts.note: surface reading: someone called Tom exits as the monarch arrives
setter's reading: a tom is a male cat and a queen a female one, both using the same small door

explanation.surface: A man named Tom slips away just as the Queen arrives at a function.
explanation.walkthrough: A tom is a male cat and a queen is the name for a female cat.
explanation.definitionFit: This small hinged door set in a house door lets pet felines come and go freely.

clue.text: Best to have no outsiders with lions about and be in control

indicators.note: 'about' means the group of lions goes around the kept letters

parts.note: a pride is a group of lions

indicators.note: having no outsiders means losing the first and last letters, keeping only the core

parts.note: the inner letters of the word

explanation.surface: The top dog among lions must stand apart to stay in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: PR(ES)IDE.
explanation.definitionFit: To chair a meeting or occupy the position of authority is to be in charge of proceedings.

clue.text: See 6 down
See 20

parts.note: surface reading: a pointer to another clue in the grid
setter's reading: this light completes the two-word phrase defined by the clue at 20 across

explanation.walkthrough: This light has no clue of its own: 20 across's clue defines the whole phrase WOLF WHISTLE, and this entry supplies its second word.
explanation.definitionFit: Together with the word at 20 across it names the shrill two-note call aimed at an attractive woman.

clue.text: Heard evidence for woman's appeal that PC won't accept

definitions.text: Heard evidence for woman's appeal that PC won't accept

parts.note: surface reading: spoken testimony in support of a woman's legal appeal
setter's reading: an audible signal that a man finds a woman attractive, frowned on by the politically correct

explanation.surface: A woman's court appeal rests on hearsay that a police constable refuses to accept.
explanation.walkthrough: This clue defines the two-word phrase completed by 19 down's WHISTLE; 'PC' is politically correct, not police constable.
explanation.definitionFit: A wolf whistle is a two-note whistle aimed at an attractive woman, now regarded as sexist.

clue.text: Hen party finally inhibited by genuine cock-up

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' turns the word for genuine upside down
being inhibited means being held in, so the single letter sits inside

parts.note: genuine means real

indicators.note: 'finally' means only the last letter of the word for party is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A hen party ends in a genuine fiasco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hen' suggests a party for a bride, but it is a bird that lays eggs; 'cock-up' is British slang for a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen kept for eggs is called this, from the verb meaning to produce eggs.

clue.text: Failing to understand, be embarrassed receiving Oscar?

indicators.note: 'receiving' means the phrase for being embarrassed takes in the name

parts.note: taken as written
Oscar Wilde, the Irish playwright
red in the face with embarrassment

explanation.surface: An actor blushes on receiving an Academy Award, not quite grasping why he won.
explanation.walkthrough: BE RED holds WILDE. 'Oscar' suggests the film award, but it is the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being utterly confused and puzzled means one fails to grasp what is going on.

clue.text: Bob's next to nominate Thomas

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the surname that follows Bob in the name of the American singer
second meaning: the first name that names the Welsh poet Thomas

explanation.surface: Bob is next in line to put forward someone called Thomas.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob Dylan is the singer-songwriter; Dylan Thomas, the Welsh poet, took the name the singer adopted.
explanation.definitionFit: The word serves as surname of the folk singer Bob and as forename of the poet Thomas.

clue.text: See 14 across
Where change is made in production of sterling quality

definitions.text: Where change is made in production of sterling quality

parts.note: surface reading: a place where alterations happen
setter's reading: small coins, minted in pounds sterling by the national coin-maker

explanation.surface: A workshop where reforms are turned out to a top standard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' is loose coins and 'sterling' is British currency, as well as meaning excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Mint is the British body that manufactures the coins of the pound sterling.

clue.text: One called in rejected unconvincing message

indicators.note: something rejected is turned back, so the word for unconvincing is read backwards
'called in' means brought inside, so the numeral goes into the other word

parts.note: a lame excuse is an unconvincing one
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A weak message was turned down after someone was summoned to deal with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Electronic mail is a message sent between computers over a network.

clue.text: For this one needs sugar daddy to abandon translation of papyrus

indicators.note: a translation renders words in another form, so what is left is rearranged
to abandon is to leave behind, so the father's word is dropped from the longer word

parts.note: taken as written
pa is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A sugar daddy deserts a scholar translating an ancient papyrus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sugar daddy' reads as one phrase but splits: sugar belongs to the definition, daddy to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet thick liquid is made by dissolving sugar in water, so sugar is its essential ingredient.

clue.text: Never leaves off advertising such growth

definitions.text: Never leaves off advertising such growth

parts.note: surface reading: an advertiser who never stops promoting
setter's reading: a plant whose leaves never come off in winter

explanation.surface: A company that never stops advertising enjoys continual expansion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves off' sounds like stopping, but here it is foliage that never falls.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants of this kind keep their foliage all year round instead of shedding it in autumn.
